title: Israel says it has destroyed major underground Hezbollah base
description: Israel's military says it has destroyed a large underground complex operated by Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.  It said it used more than 1,000 tonnes
body: Israel's military says it has destroyed a large underground complex operated by Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.  It said it used more than 1,000 tonnes of explosives to destroy two tunnels spanning more than 2km (1.2 miles) beneath the Ali Taher Ridge. The blast triggered seismic activity equivalent to a magnitude 4.1 earthquake, according to the US Geological Survey.There was no immediate public response from Hezbollah or the Lebanese government.Israeli forces took control of the ridge last week after months of fighting with the Iran-backed group there. The Israeli military occupies a large swathe of southern Lebanon captured after the conflict with Hezbollah resumed in March.Images released by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF)  showed a fireball lighting up the sky."The sky lit up and about 15 seconds later we heard the terrifying sound," Ahamed, a resident in Nabatieh, about 6km west of the ridge, told the BBC."The house shook all together as if it was literally an earthquake."He said people were screaming and children were crying, and that cars filled the roads as people left the area for Beirut.Tremors were even felt in the coastal city of Saida 40km north.The IDF said the underground infrastructure included a command centre used by Hezbollah's Badr unit and contained dozens of rockets, missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as anti-tank weapons, mines and explosives."This was strategic infrastructure that was constructed over two decades, funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime," the IDF said in a statement on Telegram."All of the terrorists who were inside the infrastructure were eliminated or fled."The IDF said the destruction of the complex completed a mission to destroy eight tunnels and establish a "security zone" in the area.The latest action comes amid renewed fighting in southern Lebanon, where Israeli forces have expanded operations against Hezbollah positions and continue to hold what Israel describes as a security zone near the border.Lebanese media reported fresh Israeli strikes elsewhere in the south on Thursday, including Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Mansouri in the Tyre district.The Lebanese army has increased deployments in areas outside Israeli control, including the southern city of Nabatieh, in efforts to strengthen stability and reassure residents, local television station MTV reported.Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader.Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory.Fighting decreased following a ceasefire deal between Iran and the US in June, alongside a separate agreement between Lebanon and Israel. The UN says about 330,000 people in Lebanon remain displaced by the conflict, with Israeli military activity, air strikes, destruction and restrictions on returning to Israeli-occupied areas preventing many from going home.Under the Lebanon-Israel framework, Hezbollah is expected to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area. Hezbollah was not directly involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations.Despite a reduction in fighting, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued.At least 4,383 people - including 395 women and 259 children - have been killed in Lebanon by Israeli attacks since 2 March, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians. At least 29 have been killed this week, the ministry says.Israeli authorities say 40 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed in the same period.Additional reporting by Raffi Berg in London and Samantha Granville and Ghaith Solh in Beirut

title: Princess Diana's 'revenge dress' goes up for auction
description: A dress worn by Princess Diana dubbed her "revenge dress" is being put up for auction.The late Princess of Wales wore the strapless black silk evening
body: A dress worn by Princess Diana dubbed her "revenge dress" is being put up for auction.The late Princess of Wales wore the strapless black silk evening dress to a party in London hours after her then-estranged husband Prince Charles admitted to committing adultery during their marriage.Her dramatic arrival at the Serpentine Gallery in 1994 in the outfit became an iconic pop-culture moment.Auction house Sotheby's expects the dress to sell for up to £220,000 ($300,000) when it goes under the hammer on 9 December - the first time it has been up for auction since 1997, when the princess sold 79 of her dresses just months before her death to raise money for charities.Morgane Halimi, Sotheby's global head of handbags and fashion, said in a statement that Princess Diana "understood instinctively" that fashion can be a language in its own right."On her own terms, Princess Diana turned the dress into one of the most powerful messages she ever made, during one of the most scrutinised and emotionally charged episodes of her life," she said."She walked into a moment in which so much of her story was being told for her and, through what she chose to wear, reclaimed the narrative for herself."The same evening as the Serpentine Gallery fundraising dinner, a documentary had aired in which the Prince of Wales (now King) had admitted that he had been unfaithful to Diana, after years of rumours and media reports.The content of the ITV interview had been leaked a few days prior, meaning Diana's first public appearance after it aired was widely interpreted as her reply.Anna Harvey, her stylist at the time, has been reported as saying that the princess "wanted to look a million dollars".She made a last-minute wardrobe change before heading out to the event, setting aside a less striking Valentino gown in favour of the off-the-shoulder dress with an asymmetric hemline and chiffon train by Greek designer Christina Stambolian, which she accessorised with a royal necklace, black clutch and black heels.The "revenge dress" will be toured around the world prior to its sale, appearing at Sotheby's London showroom from 18 to 24 September, before heading to Hong Kong for the start of October, Geneva for the start of November and then on to New York, where it will be sold. It was last auctioned by Diana herself, as one of dozens of items sold to raise funds for cancer and Aids charities.The dress was bought by then-Glasgow resident Briege Mackenzie and her husband Graeme, who paid £39,098 for it.She told the Independent, external at the time that they had purchased the item not to wear - "I can't fit in it," she said - but because the proceeds were going to charity Children First.Mackenzie said in a statement issued by Sotheby's on Thursday: "My late husband and I knew that this dress was something special. "Princess Diana was walking into the worst night of her life and you would never know it to look at her. It went from a cocktail dress to a statement in the time it took to photograph her."Thirty years on, you can say the words anywhere in the world and everyone knows exactly which dress you mean."She added that she had decided to sell the dress following the death of her husband, with whom bidding on it had been "one of the great days of our life together".Sotheby's said that a rare copy of the 1997 auction catalogue, signed by Diana and Stambolian, and which credits Prince William for the idea to auction the dress, will be sold alongside it.Part of the proceeds from the sale will be donated to Royal Edinburgh Hospital via the NHS Lothian Charity.The vintage Jaguar XJ40 car that Diana had arrived at the Serpentine Gallery event in was sold at auction earlier this year for £66,250.The dress, however, is expected to fetch a considerably higher price - though it would not be the first time an item from the princess's wardrobe has sold for a significant sum.One of Diana's sweaters, featuring a black sheep among rows of white ones, was sold for £920,000 at an auction by Sotheby's in New York in 2023.

schema.headline: Princess Diana's 'revenge dress' goes up for auction

title: More than 20 children killed in DR Congo school fire
description: At least 24 schoolchildren have died in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democrat
body: At least 24 schoolchildren have died in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, officials there have said.Adults are also reported to have died in the fire and there are fears that the death toll could rise further in the densely populated Kadutu commune.Survivors have been taken to nearby hospitals, and footage of the scene shows children lying on hospital floors in pain. Some 300 houses have also been destroyed in the fire, the cause of which is unknown.Rebel‑appointed authorities released a provisional death toll of 24 on Thursday evening, confirming previous reports, but there are fears that more people may have died.Pictures circulating on social media show young children lying motionless on the ground.A witness quoted by Reuters news agency said the fire had been put out by afternoon but smoke was still rising from rubble and corrugated metal.Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province and one of DR Congo's most crowded hillside cities, was captured by M23 rebels in February last year. Meanwhile the government in Kinshasa released a statement on X, without specifying numbers of casualties."The Ministry of National Education and New Citizenship expressed deep sorrow over the deadly fire," it said."With several lives lost and many injured, the toll remains provisional. The minister offered condolences, affirmed solidarity with families, and ordered assessments of affected schools to ensure learning continuity."The tragedy follows a similar fire in Kinshasa last weekend, where residents died in a stampede at a wedding banquet hall. In response, the government has ordered strict safety measures and deployed teams nationwide to enforce standards at public gathering places.

schema.headline: More than 20 children killed in DR Congo school fire

title: Hong Kong's Tiananmen activists sentenced to up to seven years in prison
description: Three Hong Kong activists who organised annual vigils commemorating Beijing's 1989 crackdown on Tiananmen Square protests have been handed prison sent
body: Three Hong Kong activists who organised annual vigils commemorating Beijing's 1989 crackdown on Tiananmen Square protests have been handed prison sentences of up to seven years.Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, were convicted last month of inciting others to subvert state power, under the city's controversial national security law. A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, had pleaded guilty in January.The office of United Nations human rights chief Volker Türk called for "these sentences to be quashed".Hong Kong and Macau were for years the only places on Chinese soil where people could hold gatherings to mark the Tiananmen crackdown - a highly sensitive and heavily censored topic in mainland China.These gatherings were banned by Hong Kong's authorities in 2020, citing Covid-19 policies, but never resumed. That same year, the national security law, which makes illegal a wider range of dissenting acts, officially came into force.Authorities say the law is necessary to maintain stability, but critics argue it has eroded Hong Kong's autonomy and created a climate of fear.Lee, Chow and Ho were charged in 2021. They faced up to 10 years in prison after their conviction.On Friday, the court sentenced Lee to seven years in prison, while Chow was handed seven years and three months. Ho, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to five years in prison.As the court session started, Chow and Lee stood up and smiled at the public gallery, which was full of people. Ho wore a serious expression. After their sentences were handed down, Lee appeared to pray as he was led out of the dock, while Chow blew a kiss to those seated in the public gallery.According to a court summary in August, Lee and Chow had "incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power".Chow told the court in May the law itself was on trial.A key part of the trial concerned the group's slogan of "ending one-party dictatorship", which the court said had incited people to undermine the Chinese Communist Party.Lee's wife, Elizabeth Tang, told Reuters that it was a "sad day" for her."I cannot imagine that he has to spend another three years in jail, it is really unacceptable," she said, adding that Lee intended to appeal his sentence.Chow's mother Medina told a crowd outside the court not to be "overly saddened" about the verdict. "Do not lose heart. And above all, do not feel guilty," she said, Reuters reported.Speaking to the BBC before her arrest in 2022, Chow said she was "prepared to be arrested" and "willing to pay the price for fighting for democracy".The defendants were leaders of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, a group founded in May 1989 to support students holding pro-democracy rallies.Weeks later, the Chinese Communist Party sent troops and tanks to crush pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square. Estimates of the death toll range from a few hundred to many thousands.Over the next three decades, the Hong Kong Alliance called on authorities to accept responsibility for the crackdown, free dissidents and introduce democratic reform.The group also held yearly vigils commemorating the Tiananmen Square crackdown. Organisers said some of the gatherings attracted more than 100,000 people, though police had lower estimates of the turnout.On Friday, the court also handed a HK$1.5m fine ($191,000; £142,000) to the Hong Kong Alliance. "This sentencing is a triple tragedy: for the activists being unjustly punished; the survivors and victims of the Tiananmen crackdown itself; and the generations of Hongkongers denied the space to discuss one of the most consequential events in modern Chinese history," said Amnesty International's Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks. "The harsh sentences against peaceful Tiananmen vigil organisers expose the cruelty and insecurity of a government afraid of memory and the people," Human Rights Watch said in a statement.

schema.headline: Hong Kong's Tiananmen activists sentenced to up to seven years in prison

title: Philippine rescuers board burning ferry 40 hours after blaze began
description: They finally got on at about 11:30 local time (03:30 GMT) on Friday, the coast guard said."The biggest challenge for us really is to penetrate the shi
body: They finally got on at about 11:30 local time (03:30 GMT) on Friday, the coast guard said."The biggest challenge for us really is to penetrate the ship [as] there is still a visible, thick smoke," the coastguard's spokeswoman Noemie Cayabyab told the BBC earlier."No matter how we try to push through, high temperatures and toxic smoke remain a severe risk to our personnel," she told local media earlier.Smoke resulting from incomplete burning contains dense, lethal concentrations of carbon monoxide. Earlier, authorities reported that 86 were still unaccounted for, but as of Friday morning, the figure stood at 84 – two passengers whose names were on the ship's manifest did not go onboard, authorities say.Rescuers have widened their search area, Cayabyab says, adding that the coastguard has deployed one of its largest ships and done radio broadcasts to vessels in the area. The search teams are also accompanied by divers and nurses.A local diver in Coron told the BBC on Friday that he and his team were on standby to help out and awaiting instructions from the coast guard.The coast guard also conducted an aerial survey of waters near the disaster site. The plan is to resume firefighting efforts, first from the cargo hold of the ferry, which is the compartment where containers and or goods are stored, Cayabyab said. Earlier, the coastguard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that was where the fire started. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat had described the frantic cries on board the passenger-cargo vessel when the fire erupted on Wednesday evening.Roland Lerma recalled falling while scrambling to get off the burning boat."When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," the 30-year-old told the BBC.He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea. Lerma said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark."It was cold [in the sea] If the rescue had been delayed, I would definitely have died," he said.The ferry, which set off from Manila, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, in the province of Palawan, when it caught fire.The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry."Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.

schema.headline: Philippine rescuers board burning ferry 40 hours after blaze began

title: Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons
description: Anthropic says it has identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological
body: Anthropic says it has identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons.The findings, made in the firm's recent threat intelligence report, is the latest in a growing series of warnings from AI researchers and industry insiders about the technology's potential risks to humanity.The warnings have prompted calls to action, with US Senator Bernie Sanders demanding a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence.President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position".The company published its latest threat intelligence report, external on Thursday. Such reports have become a regular feature across the AI industry as firms seek to demonstrate how they identify and disrupt attempts to misuse their models.This includes Google, which wrote on Tuesday, external that a person had attempted to use its AI tool, Gemini, to obtain a "complete, step-by-step technical guide for synthesizing weaponised biological agents".Claude, Anthropic's AI model was also used by actors linked to a Russia-based cyber espionage campaign and by an Iranian propaganda institution, according to its report.The cases of concern detected over the past eight months ranged from fake dating apps and hotel Wifi scams, to surveillance built to identify dissidents.Anthropic has also accused Chinese AI firms of trying to replicate Claude's capabilities. The lengthy report lists cases in which suspected state-sponsored groups, criminals, spyware vendors, state propaganda institutions and politically motivated individuals misused its technology."Malicious use" of its Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus models was disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, it said.None of the misuse cases involved Claude Fable or the powerful Mythos-class models, with the exception of one instance of distillation - the process for training smaller AI models using larger, more expensive models.As well as detecting the use of its models for cyber and influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud and weapon development, Anthropic said it had blocked scientists who used its AI in ways that could support biological weapons development.The report highlighted "five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development".Biological misuse, it said, is "one of the most serious risks of frontier AI model". Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities "could have catastrophic consequences", Anthropic said."The same information that can be used to develop a biological weapon could also be used to develop, for example, a vaccine or a cure for a disease," Anthropic said.Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, told the New York Times, external it was "an incredibly nuanced situation"."You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, 'Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,'" he said.The report also noted six cases where Claude was used "to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs, and other munitions, as well as the targeting and control systems that operate them".The report indicated that cybercriminals and state-backed hackers have increasingly used its technology to assist their operations.Hacking group ShinyHunters, as well as China-based labs, were among those named in the report.The report also said that a hacking group whose work is consistent with the Russia-based Midnight Blizzard allegedly used AI to build a system that automatically detected when its malware was flagged by security defences and rewrote code until it evaded detection.The California-based company said it had incorporated its findings into its processes "to better prevent, detect, and disrupt these activities in the future".Anthropic said it had shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners where appropriate.The report - the company's first this year - comes after a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned AI is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.In an article published on 6 September, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki called for the industry to implement "voluntary slowdowns" until safeguards are set."I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence," Pachocki said, adding that OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, will continue its work on building safeguards, though broader interventions are required.The warning prompted an open letter to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham calling for a new multinational treaty for the safe development of AI and a call for governments to collaborate about what a treaty based on the development of superintelligence should look like.In the US, Democratic lawmaker Bernie Sanders has introduced legislation to ban AI  superintelligence and temporarily pause advanced AI development."When scientists tell you there is a chance, a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he said on Thursday on BBC's Newsnight.With additional reporting from Osmond Chia.

schema.headline: Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons

title: Abhijeet Dipke, CJP: The student behind 'cockroach' protests that forced an Indian minister to quit
description: In just under three months, 30-year-old Abhijeet Dipke - the founder and face of India's Gen Z "cockroach" protests - has acquired the kind of celebri
body: In just under three months, 30-year-old Abhijeet Dipke - the founder and face of India's Gen Z "cockroach" protests - has acquired the kind of celebrity status normally reserved for a breakout actor or cricketer.In politics or activism, unless you come from an influential family, such recognition can take years - if it comes at all."It's been a rollercoaster ride. Two-three months ago, nobody knew me. I was just in my room in Boston watching documentaries or attending lectures," said Dipke, who recently completed a master's in public relations at Boston University."Now I'm here surrounded by hundreds of people, by cameras. It's a bit overwhelming."In and around his hometown of Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in the western state of Maharashtra, Dipke is routinely thronged by people wanting to shake his hand or take a photo.If the attention bothers him, it doesn't show. Perhaps because politics isn't entirely new to him: before moving to the US, Dipke had worked with the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), an opposition party that grew out of an anti-corruption movement, for three years.Then, on 16 May, Dipke wrote a post on X that would change his life: "What if all cockroaches come together?"It was a response to a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to cockroaches. Kant later said his comments had been misinterpreted and were directed specifically at young people using fake degrees, rather than the country's youth more broadly.But the clarification did little to quell the outrage.Dipke said he wrote his post while playing a video game. "It was totally spontaneous. I had no idea it would become such a big movement," he said.Encouraged by tens of thousands of responses, he joined a handful of former colleagues and activists to launch the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), its name playing on both the chief justice's remark and that of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).Alongside the support, Dipke and the campaign were fiercely trolled by government supporters. Their website and X account was briefly taken down in India. Dipke says that when he wrote to X and to India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology asking why the account had been taken down, he received a notice saying it had been withheld under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act which allows the government to block online information 'in the interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State'. The ministry did not reply to the BBC's questions about the issue, but The Indian Express and other media reported government officials as saying the sites had been blocked because of 'national security concerns'. Dipke says he decided to return to India in response to this."I took the decision to come back to India when I was called a national security threat by my own government. That really hurt me. Isn't my government supposed to stand by me when I'm abroad?" he said. "I decided I need to go back to my country to show I'm not a national security threat. I love my country, just not in the way that you [the government] want."Returning was not an easy decision. In recent years, activists and journalists critical of the government have faced police questioning, legal cases and, in some instances, jail.Dipke says a lawyer he consulted advised him against returning, warning that he could be detained under the National Security Act (NSA), which allows detention without formal charge or trial. The government has always denied it takes retaliatory action but a fear of reprisal prevails."I won't lie. I was afraid. I had sleepless nights thinking if I go back to India, my life will change. But if I sit in the US, all these people who have followed the Cockroach Janta Party, they will feel betrayed - that 'he didn't come to India, he just kept hiding in the US'," said Dipke.His family was worried too."My mother broke down over a phone call. She said, 'Why are you coming back? They might put you in jail or attack you.' I told her I can't backtrack now because people will mock me."The cockroach protests were not the first mass agitation Modi's government has faced. Thousands protested against a controversial citizenship law in 2019 and against farm laws introduced in 2020.Those movements were often portrayed by government supporters as representing particular religious or political interests, or as attempts to damage India's image.Attempts to discredit the cockroach protests in similar ways, however, gained less traction for a number of reasons.Despite India's impressive economic growth, education and employment remain major concerns for young Indians. A recent government report found that just over 8% of graduates find jobs aligned with their skills. The unemployment rate for graduates stands at 29.1% - a rate nine times higher than for those who never attended school.And after more than 12 years in power, Modi's government is facing anti-incumbency in a way it didn't back in 2020.But, crucially, the CJP also found an issue with broad appeal.Around the time the campaign began, the national medical entrance exam was scrapped after a question-paper leak. The scandal resonated with students and middle-class families, cutting across religious and caste lines. More than 20 students were reported to have taken their own lives in its aftermath.Dipke says focusing on the leak was not a strategic decision, but a response to students who reached out to the CJP."I was speaking to at least a hundred followers every day, and most of them were complaining about the paper leak. There was this core frustration around it," he said.When the CJP first protested at Delhi's Jantar Mantar on 6 June, the turnout was in hundreds, but nowhere near enough for it to be considered a serious movement on the ground."But the longer we sat, the more people started trusting us," Dipke said. He credits activist Sonam Wangchuk's 26-day hunger strike for galvanising support.Then came a turning point.On 20 July, when protesters attempted to march towards parliament, police and paramilitary forces used tear gas, batons and pellet guns to disperse them. Dozens of protesters were injured; the government says dozens of police personnel were also wounded.Images of young protesters being met with force triggered a surge of support. Thousands began arriving at Jantar Mantar and demonstrations spread to other cities.Opposition parties rallied behind the CJP. Asked whether he challenged their leaders over why they had not taken up students' concerns more forcefully, Dipke said he had not."This was the first time I was organising a protest so I was just grateful to them for coming out in support of us."The government was suddenly on the back foot. On two successive nights, Modi released videos addressing the country's youth, saying that tough action would be taken against those involved in exam leaks. But they fuelled further backlash because he wasn't offering what the protesters wanted: the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.It seemed almost unthinkable that Pradhan, a core BJP leader who had played an important role in recent regional elections, would be compelled to go.On 25 July, however, he stepped down, saying it was "to ensure that anti-national elements do not take advantage of the situation".Modi's government had reversed course before - most notably when it repealed three farm laws in 2021 after a year of protests. But this climbdown had come remarkably quickly, at the hands of a movement led by people who had been largely unknown only weeks earlier.Dipke was on stage at the protest site when the news reached him. He dropped to his knees, then sprang up, punched his fist into the air and shouted: "We have done it."Now that the euphoria of that moment has passed, the CJP is confronting more difficult questions - not least how to hold on to the attention it captured.Its latest campaign focuses on conditions in government schools in rural India."What I'm hoping to accomplish is that children in rural India should at least get a dignified education," said Dipke during a visit to a school in Maharashtra's Hingoli district.The school had no toilet for female students and expired food packets were being used to prepare lunches. At another, cracks ran through the floors, walls and ceiling.The campaign has gained some traction, but feels more ad-hoc than a planned national movement, and the CJP still resembles a loose pressure group - something Dipke says is deliberate."People have limited politics just to elections and political parties. We want to move beyond that," he said. "What we are here for is a cultural transformation where people understand their rights, their duties, and how to hold the government accountable no matter which party comes to power."There are also questions about what the movement chooses to fight for.Dipke is a Dalit, from a community once considered untouchable and placed at the bottom of India's rigid caste hierarchy. Quotas in jobs and education for lower castes remain deeply polarising.Over the past decade, India has also seen increasing Islamophobia and deepening religious divides.Some critics accuse the CJP of avoiding contentious issues affecting Muslims and lower-caste Indians for fear of alienating Hindu supporters. Dipke rejects this."I was really happy when, at Jantar Mantar, I used to chant 'Jai Bhim', thousands of other people followed," he said, referring to a slogan associated with Dalit icon BR Ambedkar. "We were also chanting 'Hindu-Muslim politics will not work anymore'."For now, the bigger test is whether the CJP can turn the extraordinary burst of anger that propelled it into national prominence into something that lasts.For Dipke, a self-confessed introvert thrust suddenly into public life, the test is also intensely personal."I'm the kind of person who would rather spend most of the day alone in my room," he said. "But now I'm out here among hundreds of people, doing what I must to keep this movement alive - and to sustain the hope they have placed in us."Additional reporting by Adnan Bhat and Prem Boominathan

schema.headline: Abhijeet Dipke, CJP: The student behind 'cockroach' protests that forced an Indian minister to quit

title: Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane
description: Yemen's Houthis have claimed a major advance on the western Red Sea coast, consolidating their grip on the key international shipping route.The Iran-b
body: Yemen's Houthis have claimed a major advance on the western Red Sea coast, consolidating their grip on the key international shipping route.The Iran-backed group seized Perim Island at the mouth of the waterway in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a source from Yemen's internationally-recognised government told the BBC.It comes a day after the Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, according to military sources. A Yemeni military official told the AFP news agency the Houthis now control the entire coastline.The Houthis earlier said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated their threat to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis during their rapid advance, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News - the BBC's media partner in North America.Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.A senior Trump administration official later told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."On Friday, Yemeni pro-government forces withdrew from Perim (also known as Mayyun). Witnesses and news agencies reported that Houthi forces moved on to the island.The Houthis later issued a statement, saying that their military operation to expel Saudi-backed forces had been a "success" and that "maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels".Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the "large-scale" military operation was launched on 3 September due to Saudi Arabia's "blatant aggression" against "our dear people".Sarea also said the Houthis had expelled "Saudi enemy" forces from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, claiming that hundreds of troops had been killed, wounded or captured. The Houthi statement, however, did not mention Perim Island.Saudi Arabia has not publicly commented on the latest developments.Perim Island sits at the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which has become increasingly important following the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz - another crucial waterway - in the conflict between the US and Iran.Saudi Arabia has been relying on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait for shipping oil to customers in Asia. The escalation of the conflict between the Houthis, Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia has contributed to a surge in oil prices.Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed and thousands displaced since the Houthis launched an offensive in the south-west a week ago.A Saudi-led coalition has also carried out air strikes on Houthi-controlled areas in western Yemen in support of the pro-government forces, and the Houthis have launched missiles and drones at cities and oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia.Since fighting escalated, at least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).On Friday, the IOM said the number was "alarmingly rising by the hour". Amy Pope, IOM director general, said: "Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left."The Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government in 2015, triggering Saudi military intervention in the civil war. The group currently control much of Yemen, including the capital Sanaa. A truce that had largely held for more than four years effectively collapsed in July.

schema.headline: Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane

title: Man jailed after threatening to behead son's teacher in French village
description: A man has been given a six-month jail term in France after he threatened to behead a female primary school teacher who had disciplined his son at a vi
body: A man has been given a six-month jail term in France after he threatened to behead a female primary school teacher who had disciplined his son at a village primary school.The 47-year-old was sentenced after a fast-track hearing on Thursday, six days after the events unfolded in Le Fauga, a village with a population of about 2,600 just outside the southwestern city of Toulouse.The teacher has been granted official protection and has gone on sick leave.French Education Minister Edouard Geffray said: "No teacher should be afraid to do their job. Attacking one of them is attacking the entire institution."Over the summer, Geffray steered through a law aimed at protecting staff from a "significant risk" to their safety or health from a member of a student's family. The minister said this case would trigger one of the first uses of the decree.The case revives terrible memories in France of the beheading of a teacher in the Paris suburb of Conflans-Sainte-Honorine six years ago. Samuel Paty was murdered in a jihadist attack outside his school by an 18-year-old Chechen refugee.In Le Fauga, the teacher's colleagues did not go into work on Monday because of what had happened the previous Friday.The threat was made after the man had been called in for a chat with the school, according to Toulouse education chief Karim Benmiloud.Le Fauga Mayor Jean-Marie Puig told BFMTV that the man's son had been disruptive in class and he had been sent to another class to calm down.The child continued to misbehave in the second classroom and the teacher later told him off for acting up.The teacher was later threatened by the father, who according to the mayor had waited for her "outside the school and apparently threatened to cut off her head if she'd been a man".The parent subsequently apologised, however a judicial complaint was made and he went before a judge in Toulouse on Thursday afternoon.According to French reports from the court in Toulouse, the judge told the man that  such remarks were disturbing, particularly in light of the Samuel Paty case, "which remains fresh in the minds of all French people".The Toulouse prosecutor had asked for a period of six months' house arrest, however the judge said the man should serve the time in jail because of the seriousness of his actions."I'm really not proud of myself," the man said, according to the prosecutor's team.The sentence also requires him to undergo a citizenship course and avoid contacting the victim or approaching the school.The decree passed in July allows for a student to be transferred to another school in a case involving significant risk to staff, and where education authorities have intervened.It is thought the boy and a younger sister may now be moved to another school outside Le Fauga.The teacher involved, who is in her 50s, is said to be very shocked by the threat.

schema.headline: Man jailed after threatening to behead son's teacher in French village

title: Black Axe in South Africa: Six Nigerians Nigerians accused of romance scams to be extradited to the US
description: Black Axe is a shadowy criminal network known for its extreme violence and operates across Africa, Europe and North America.A BBC Eye investigation in
body: Black Axe is a shadowy criminal network known for its extreme violence and operates across Africa, Europe and North America.A BBC Eye investigation in 2021 suggested that the syndicate had become one of the most far-reaching and dangerous organised crime groups in the world.Nigeria is its main recruitment ground and many of its members are university educated and inducted during their schooling.The group has been on the radar of law enforcement agencies for a number of years.FBI operations against Black Axe were launched in November 2019 and September 2021, eventually charging more than 35 individuals with multi-million dollar internet fraud. Since then there have been several other operations across multiple countries targeting Black Axe co-ordinated by the global policing agency Interpol.Last month, Interpol said during its latest one - which took place between November 2025 and June 2026 - seven sites in South Africa linked to a syndicate involved in romance and investment scams were raided.It led to the arrests of 39 people, the seizure of money and the blocking of more than 250 bank accounts.

schema.headline: Black Axe in South Africa: Six Nigerians Nigerians accused of romance scams to be extradited to the US

title: Four takeaways from Trump's speech at midterms convention
description: Four key takeaways from  Republican midterms conventionFigure caption, Watch: Trump tells supporters their vote will decide if country "stumbles" or "
body: Four key takeaways from  Republican midterms conventionFigure caption, Watch: Trump tells supporters their vote will decide if country "stumbles" or "moves forward"ByDaniel Bush Washington correspondent, reporting from Dallas The Republican Party's first midterms convention had all the trappings of the traditional presidential election-year gathering: supporters in sparkling costumes, a conveyor belt of candidate speeches, and vendors selling campaign merchandise.But unlike an ordinary convention, no official party business was conducted in Dallas, with the event instead serving as a rally for Republicans who are seeking to boost turnout and avoid losing control of Congress in November.President Donald Trump, whose grip over the party remains absolute, delivered a lengthy keynote speech on Wednesday during the opening night of the two-day event. He covered many of the subjects he has returned to time and again this year - with a few surprises thrown in.Here are the key takeaways from his address.1. Preaching to the MAGA choirThe vast arena was filled with diehard Trump supporters sporting red MAGA gear from his past presidential campaigns. A decade after his first White House run, Trump is still beloved among his base and he has bent the party to his will in the years since.The old-style Republican establishment, or what's left of it in the Trump era, was nowhere to be seen. Senator Susan Collins of Maine and other Republicans running in competitive races chose to stay away. Image source, Getty ImagesThe absence of more moderate Republicans was glaring and offered a reminder of just how much the party has changed.It also raised questions about the effectiveness of holding an unprecedented midterm convention in the first place. The core audience, both in the arena and watching on television, appeared to be Trump loyalists, not the moderates and swing voters the Republican Party needs to turn out in large numbers in November.2. Trump offers $5,000 payoutFigure caption, Watch: Trump says US adults will get $5,000 if Republicans win midtermsTrump has long thrown out unconventional ideas at rallies. On Wednesday night, that came in the form of an offer to pay every adult US citizen $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November.The only caveat, Trump said, was the money would have to be spent in the US.He offered no details on how the plan would work, where the money would come from, or how the US government would monitor how it was spent. Democrats quickly labelled it an "empty promise" and others questioned whether such a pledge was even legal.There are nearly 270 million American adults, which means a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.Whether the plan was possible or not appeared to be beside the point. The idea drew raucous applause at the convention and Trump seemed to relish the moment.3. A gamble on affordabilityEarlier on Wednesday, as he departed for the convention, Trump acknowledged that Americans may have to wait a while longer to see relief from high fuel prices."I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterms," Trump said.The president reiterated that message in his speech, arguing that short-term economic pain caused by the war in Iran was worth it to prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.But that may be a difficult message to land with voters who are feeling higher prices.Figure caption, Watch: Do Republicans blame Trump for high oil prices?Polls have consistently indicated in recent months that the cost of living is a top-ranking issue among Americans.Trump's approval rating, too, has taken a hit as the war in Iran has dragged on. A Financial Times / Focaldata poll released on Sunday indicated that it had hit a new low, with only 33% of registered voters approving of his presidential performance.Many Republican candidates may well have hoped for a more direct message on addressing the cost of living and quickly ending the war in Iran.4. It's still Trump's party Trump's total grip on the party raises some pointed questions about its future. Namely - who will replace him? And more immediately for November's elections, how will it perform when his name isn't on the ballot?Image source, Getty ImagesTrump offered a simple solution to the latter question on Wednesday night. After warning that the sitting president tends to lose the midterms, he told the crowd: "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot."The remark was an acknowledgement by Trump that he remains the party's best driver of turnout. It also speaks to the challenge Republicans have both in November and in the next presidential election in 2028.Trump will not be on the ballot again, and though he can continue campaigning for the party, there is not a clear or obvious successor who can rally the base quite like Trump.In interviews with the BBC, convention goers often looked ahead to the election in two years' time and debated who Trump's successor should be. Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were frequently mentioned as top contenders.Trump, however, made clear in Dallas that he is still in charge and is not in a hurry to give up the spotlight.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Four takeaways from Trump's speech at midterms convention

title: Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches
description: Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found,
body: Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found, escalating its use of a weapon that Kyiv's air defences are struggling to deal with.It marked the first time that daily attacks by Moscow's new upgraded Geran drones were recorded in Ukrainian Air Force data. The growing use of jet-propelled and other varieties of drones prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to condemn what he called an unfolding "horror" over the skies of Kyiv.Ukraine's military recently told the BBC that jet-powered drone attacks grew from 350 in June to 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August. In five of the nightly attacks in August, these drones outnumbered the older, slower models."The reason for turning to jet-powered drones is that they are much faster than the previous generation and it makes it much more difficult for Ukraine to intercept them," said Dr Marina Miron, an expert on military technology at King's College London.The upgraded munitions can cruise at more than 300mph, significantly faster than older models and well beyond the top speed of Kyiv's interceptors. The drones are powered by turbojet engines, some of which, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, are sourced from China.According to Zelensky, the drones were used as part of a wave of attacks that killed at least 12 people and injured 20 more on 1 September. Six of the casualties were railway workers after a depot was hit in Kyiv.And on Wednesday the Moldovan government said a plane carrying Zelensky was delayed at Chisinau airport on Tuesday after a Russian drone - reported to be jet-powered - entered Moldovan airspace.Earlier this year Ukraine showed relative success in countering Russian drones and was intercepting 94% of long-range drones, according to Zelensky. But the speed of the newer drones has prompted the latest round in Kyiv and Moscow's arms race. On 10 August, Ukraine's deputy head of military intelligence, Maj Gen Vadym Skibitskyi, said his forces needed new interceptor missiles "capable of matching [jet-drones'] speed".

schema.headline: Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches

title: Ukraine's fortress cities under fire as Russia bids to seize rest of Donbas
description: It is so dangerous now in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk that police say it is time for civilians to get out. These neighbouring cities are the biggest stil
body: It is so dangerous now in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk that police say it is time for civilians to get out. These neighbouring cities are the biggest still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region.In the worst affected areas, forced evacuations of families with children have already begun, says Pavlo Dyachenko of Donetsk police."This is the only way to save your life," he says, because security has deteriorated so much."If you take Slovyansk, it used to be hit by glide bombs roughly once a week, but now it's almost every day."Slovyansk, Kramatorsk and Kostyantynivka, to the south, form part of what is known as Ukraine's "fortress belt" – a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the east.However, Kostyantynivka only has a limited presence of Ukrainian troops left, reports say, while Russia claims to be in full control of it.Over the summer, the number of civilians wounded by Russian attacks on the two cities increased from 70 in June to 212 in August, say Ukrainian police.Sixteen people died in June, 20 in July and 15 in August.Residential housing comes under attack as well as infrastructure, says Dyachenko, causing "very significant destruction".The number of glide bombs launched by Russia jumped from 40 in June to 109 in July and 92 in August, according to data published by Ukrainian police and studied by the BBC.One morning two weeks ago, on 25 August, nine glide bombs targeted Kramatorsk. Seven hit civilian apartment blocks, wounding 24 people including a two-month-old baby, Ukrainian police say.Two days later, it was hit again, this time with seven glide bombs, and five bombs targeted Slovyansk.Fitted with winglets so they can glide to their target rather than fall, glide bombs are considered one of the most effective and lethal weapons in Russia's arsenal.Usually, they weigh 250 or 500 kg, but there have been cases of Russia deploying bombs that weigh 1,500 kg. "The devastation they cause is simply incredible," says Dyachenko."Glide bombs are the big fear," another British volunteer, John Auckland Abbey, posted on social media."They are silent killers, and when you've been abruptly woken by one exploding, you know at least another one will follow. The question you ask yourself as you lie very still in the dark is: will the next one be closer?"Kramatorsk is currently home to the headquarters of the Donetsk regional administration. The capital city used to be Donetsk, until it was captured in 2014 by Russian-backed separatists.What happens to the areas of Donbas still under Ukrainian control was reportedly a key issue when US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend after their talks with Putin.In the past, Witkoff has appeared to back Russian claims to the region, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is refusing to pull troops out of it. He says Putin has given his generals until the end of the year to complete their occupation of Donbas."Putin's primary objective on the front line remains the same: Kostyantynivka-Slovyansk," Zelensky told journalists last month.Faced with mounting military pressure, the Ukrainian leader has created two new taskforces headed by experienced generals, Andriy Biletsky and Denys Prokopenko, to defend the portion of Donbas still in Ukrainian hands."There isn't just a battle for Donbas there," one unnamed Ukrainian general has said. "What is probably the main battle of this year and the next is now unfolding."

schema.headline: Ukraine's fortress cities under fire as Russia bids to seize rest of Donbas

title: Trump shadow looms large over Brics as Modi hosts Putin and Xi in Delhi
description: The US is not a member of Brics, yet President Donald Trump's shadow will loom large over the group's summit in Delhi this weekend.Leaders from 11 Bri
body: The US is not a member of Brics, yet President Donald Trump's shadow will loom large over the group's summit in Delhi this weekend.Leaders from 11 Brics nations - including host India, China, Russia, Brazil, South Africa, the UAE and Iran, with Saudi Arabia attending as an invited member - will hold talks on a wide range of issues. But few will be as consequential as the impact of President Trump's policies.The war in Iran and the ever-present threat of White House tariffs, directed at both US adversaries and allies, have destabilised global energy markets and has often left the global economy guessing the future.It is against this backdrop that Brics leaders are meeting. Yet the group is unlikely to produce a consensus statement that openly calls out the US or lays out a coordinated strategy to counter President Trump's policies and geopolitics.That is partly because Brics itself is deeply divided over how far it should go in challenging Washington."India cannot afford to have a joint statement that rails against Washington," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC. He expects any criticism of US policies to be "vague and indirect", reflecting the sharply divergent interests within the expanded group.While Russia and Iran may push for the group to take a clearer stand against President Trump, the geopolitical realities within Brics are likely to make that difficult.India, which is reportedly in the final stages of a trade deal with the US, will not want a statement that could upset the White House. China, too, may be wary of being seen as using Brics to target Washington.Then there is the UAE, which has come under Iranian attack during Tehran's retaliation against US and Israeli strikes. The Gulf state, which hosts US military bases, is unlikely to support a statement that helps Tehran's cause.Kugelman says Brics has become more significant through its expansion, but that has also made consensus harder."You've added a number of members that don't get along," he said, describing the challenge for India as bringing together countries with "a wide array of views and positions on the global order".Trump has also been quite vocal against Brics, particularly its efforts to reduce global trade's dependence on the US dollar, commonly known as de-dollarisation.He has often warned the group against trying to come up with an alternative currency or take measures to weaken the dollar's dominance in global trade.In one such threat, Trump said in November 2024 that Brics countries would face "100% tariffs" if they backed another currency to replace the "mighty US dollar".Under these circumstances, what can the group realistically deliver?Brics' geopolitical and economic heft has grown substantially over the past decade. While it will be reluctant to take an openly anti-US or anti-Western position, the group will be looking to build on its existing achievements and demonstrate that it can emerge as an alternative blocs like the G20 and G7.Brics now accounts for 49% of the world's population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of international trade, according to BBC Monitoring's analysis.Its most tangible achievement remains the New Development Bank - which has approved billions of dollars in infrastructure and development projects - many of them in countries of the global south.The group has also created a $100bn contingency reserve arrangement to help members facing financial crises, although it has yet to be tested.The leaders are also likely to explore ways to make cross-border payments in local currencies easier. That will be of particular interest to Moscow and Tehran, both of which face severe US sanctions.Brics is also expected to continue positioning itself as a voice for the developing nations, collectively pushing for reforms to institutions such as the United Nations, International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, which many developing nations feel do not accurately reflect the new global order.For India, in particular, the summit offers an opportunity to strengthen its claim to leadership of the global south.Many of Delhi's own foreign policy priorities, including multilateralism, a more multipolar world, greater representation for developing countries and freer global trade, align closely with Brics' wider agenda.But India will also have to find ways to work around China's considerable influence within Brics and its stronger presence across much of the developing world.The Modi government has placed a strong emphasis on becoming a "leader or a voice of the Global South", Kugelman says. But India's efforts have had "limited success" in making deeper inroads in Africa and Latin America, where China has been more successful.With most Brics members coming from developing economies, Kugelman says the expanded grouping gives India an opportunity to deepen ties with countries such as Ethiopia, Brazil and Indonesia and build a stronger profile across Africa and Latin America.For Delhi, the test will be whether it can secure a consensus statement - often seen as a measure of a host nation's diplomatic success. That will be difficult given sharp differences over the Iran war, relations with the US and the future of global trade.The scale of the challenge was evident in May, when Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement after their summit because of differences over the Iran war, leaving host India to issue a chair's summary instead.India will take confidence from its experience as G20 host in 2023, when it managed to secure a joint declaration despite deep divisions over Russia's war in Ukraine.But Delhi will also want substantive announcements and to highlight what Brics has already achieved. On this, members are likely to agree: none will want the grouping dismissed as merely a "talk shop".Leaders are expected to explore ways to strengthen financial cooperation and may make substantive announcements. They are also likely to address major geopolitical developments, with any language on the US is expected to be carefully crafted to avoid confrontation.Washington, for its part, will be watching closely.The summit will also provide the setting for several important bilateral meetings. Chinese President Xi Jinping's meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday will be keenly watched. The two countries have been slowly rebuilding ties, although progress has been more cautious than either side might have hoped.Modi is also due to meet President Vladimir Putin, with the war in Ukraine likely to feature prominently in their discussions.Modi made a highly public appeal for peace when he met Putin last month on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek. While some interpreted his remarks as a rebuke to Moscow, Russia did not see them that way and publicly welcomed Modi's efforts.Beyond geopolitics, India's growing trade deficit with both Russia and China is also likely to feature in the bilateral discussions.But in the end, the group's focus will be on concluding a successful summit as it would add further weight to Brics' influence.And for host India, it would also be a diplomatic and geopolitical achievement at a time when Delhi is seeking to reassert its international influence.Kugelman says the stakes are particularly high for India at this summit.Delhi, he argues, has been somewhat overshadowed by Pakistan's recent diplomatic role in the Middle East, including its involvement in mediation efforts around the Iran war."This is an important opportunity for India to reassert its global significance and its global leadership," he says. "That is one reason why the stakes are high."The summit, he adds, is in some ways "more important for India as host than it is for the Brics grouping as a whole".

schema.headline: Trump shadow looms large over Brics as Modi hosts Putin and Xi in Delhi

title: Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult?
description: Figure caption, BBC’s Samira Hussain explains what needs to happen for Trump's $5,000 gift to become realityByAlex BoydUS President Donald Trump has o
body: Figure caption, BBC’s Samira Hussain explains what needs to happen for Trump's $5,000 gift to become realityByAlex BoydUS President Donald Trump has offered every adult American $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win November's midterm elections, but it is unclear how such a plan would be funded and whether it is legal.His remarks prompted raucous applause from supporters at a party convention on Wednesday night, although Democrats labelled it an "empty promise".Trump also told the Republican conference that the money would have to be spent in the US, but it is unclear how that would be monitored.US Vice-President JD Vance suggested it might be paid for by tariff revenue and that such cheques would not go to wealthy Americans. Is Trump's offer legal?Under US federal law, it is illegal to give payments that are intended to influence the way a person is voting.However, some experts have said the offer made by Trump in Texas on Wednesday could be seen as a pledge to cut taxes, which is legal.Dr Joan Mahoney, lecturer in law at the University of Southampton, told the BBC she thought the offer would be legal, though she said politicians "don't usually do it quite this explicitly"."On the one hand it sounds a bit like a bribe, vote for the Republicans and you'll get money, which would be decidedly illegal," she said."But on the other hand it would go to everyone, regardless of how they voted so it isn't in that sense a bribe."I think it would be legal. It's the same kind of campaign pledge as saying 'if my party wins we'll reduce taxes'. Every party does that all the time... and that's obviously perfectly legal."However, Laurel Rapp, director of the US and North America programme at Chatham House, told the BBC that Trump's offer seemed to be "a very different, very transactional agreement" from the kind of promise usually made by candidates in an election period.Figure caption, Watch: BBC North America editor Sarah Smith looks into whether Trump's promise stands upHow much would it cost?Aside from the question of legality, some have also asked whether Trump's offer would be feasible financially in the context of increasing US debt, partially as a result of the war in Iran.There are nearly 270 million American adults, meaning a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.Trump gave no details on how such cheques would be funded.Congress authorises spending in the US, but the president did not say whether he planned to ask for legislative approval for any payments. And legal experts said it was unlikely he could approve such a vast sum via a presidential executive order.Erica York, a senior economist at the Washington DC-based Tax Foundation, told the BBC she would be "extremely surprised" if Congress approved any proposal."This would be one of the worst ways to use $1.3 trillion," she said. "We're on a very unsustainable track, with deficits only projected to grow and grow," York added. Image source, EPACould tariff revenue fund it?Speaking to Fox News after Trump's speech, Vice-President Vance indicated that the payments could be funded by money raised by the president from tariffs.However, such revenue to date falls far short of the money that would be needed to account for Trump's $5,000 cheques offer.According to the Bipartisan Policy Center, the US has brought in around $475bn in tariff and excise tax revenue since the beginning of 2025. But more than $100bn has been refunded after the Supreme Court struck down many tariffs earlier this year.When asked how the payouts could work, the White House said in a statement to the BBC: "The doomers and naysayers have consistently doubted President Trump.""With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results," added spokesman Davis Ingle.Why has Trump made the offer?One former Republican strategist and pollster said Trump's latest offer should be firmly seen in the context of an election that is now less than two months away. "It is an extraordinary promise, and I'm not sure where that money is going to come from - but it is campaign season," Robert Moran told the BBC.Chatham House's Rapp said Trump was thinking short term to try to keep hold of Congress as he enters the final two years of his term in office."Money is something that he is now resorting to because the polling is not looking good for Republicans and the polling is not looking good for him," she continued.Has anything similar happened before?Trump has previously proposed $2,000 cheques to be funded by tariff revenues, but those payouts have not materialised.Former President Joe Biden was accused of buying votes when he promised $2,000 Covid stimulus cheques for Americans if Democrats won Senate elections in Georgia in January 2021.A similar controversy arose ahead of the 2024 presidential election, during which billionaire Trump supporter Elon Musk offered cash incentives to registered voters in seven swing states who signed a certain petition.Additional reporting by Bernd Debusmann Jr, White House reporter

schema.headline: Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult?
